signals.title: How I design in Figma with Claude Code: AI Design Jam session
signals.description: At our AI Jam on September 29 2026 Marco-Christian Krenn and I showed how we design in Figma with Claude Code and the Figma CLI . This is my side of the session. I started with Lovable and ended up in the terminal I have been vibe coding since March 2025. I started with Lovable. The chat was easy but I burned hundreds of dollars 🤑 a day and the result still did not look the way I wanted. Then I saw the GitHub button. I exported the project and continued in Cursor. That was cheaper. Then I found Claude Code. That was my life-changing moment. Today I ask Claude Code first for every task that does not need my body :D I am a designer with no engineering background. Marco still gives me private lessons on Git after our meetups. During the Jam my Figma CLI repo crossed 1,000 stars on GitHub. Thank you to everyone who starred it live 😍 Why I built the Figma CLI Agents are expensive. I see people burning hundreds of dollars a day on design agents. I wanted a way for Claude Code to control Figma that burns fewer tokens. The Figma CLI talks to the Figma app directly. You need no API key and no MCP server. It does not count against the Figma MCP rate limits and it uses no Figma AI credits. Most AI-in-Figma tools overload the AI’s memory An MCP server loads every tool and a wall of instructions before you say a word. The context window fills up and the agent starts to produce AI slop. I compare it to a meeting where someone bombards you with information and then asks you to execute. You don’t know where to start. Even paid Figma seats hit a limit The official Figma MCP server has rate limits. A Full seat on the Professional plan gets up to 200 tool calls a day. The table is in Figma’s docs . 200 sounds like a lot. But a tool call is not a prompt. A prompt like “update my button to use the variables from another collection” needs several calls. The agent reads the button and the variables before it changes anything and checks the result afterwards. “200 tool calls is not a lot if you do something locally with your agent.” (Marco) My token benchmark: Figma CLI vs the official Figma MCP I tested both on 26 Figma tasks that the Figma CLI was never optimized for. I took the median of 3 runs per task with Claude Code and Opus 5.5 on September 25 2026. Figma CLI: 1,701,390 tokens in 407.3 seconds Official Figma MCP: 3,531,953 tokens in 658.0 seconds The MCP used 108% more tokens than the CLI. This is my own benchmark. Figma can improve its MCP tomorrow and then the numbers change. Run your own test on your own tasks. Why I still need the canvas People ask me why I don’t build everything in code. I need the canvas to tweak things. I can’t prompt “move it a little to the left” a thousand times. So the agent builds the first version and then I push pixels myself. Marco explained why this combination works so well. You design one card by hand and the agent repeats your decisions on the other 50. “An agent can easily read what your decisions were and, like, repeat them.” How I use it every day I rarely use the Figma CLI to generate new designs. I use it to help me with the design I am already working on. What I showed in the session: Scale dozens of thumbnails or switch them from light to dark mode with one prompt Import variables in seconds Import or create DESIGN.md files and design components in that style Prompt animations with Figma Motion Run accessibility checks that I added to the CLI myself Whenever I catch myself doing a manual task in Figma I ask Claude Code to add it as a feature. Many people now run their own custom version of the CLI. You can even connect a local LLM. I designed offline on a long flight and spent $0 on tokens. You need a strong machine for that. On a MacBook with 16 GB RAM I would not try it. Three ways to connect Yolo: patches Figma Desktop once and after that everything runs automatically. figma-cli connect Safe Mode: runs as a Figma plugin and your Figma app is never modified. figma-cli connect --safe Browser: drives Figma in a normal Chrome window and leaves the desktop app untouched. figma-cli connect --browser Marco built the browser mode. Someone asked what you can break in Yolo mode. Marco’s answer: it starts Figma in a different mode and only has access to your Figma app. “Your agent has 10 times more access than the CLI.” What Marco is building next Marco is working on a new version of the CLI written in Rust. It is not released yet. In the session he showed: Multi-file editing: update a library across 20 files in one run instead of opening every file Ghost variables: a tool call that finds them and suggests replacements that are close in Delta E Checkpoints: the CLI writes a history marker before it changes a file so you can roll back One-line install: a binary that runs without Node Speed: each tool call to Figma takes 3 to 5 milliseconds Brand context makes the difference Marco ran one session with Claude Code and Opus 5.5. It created three landing pages in a couple of minutes. All three used variables and worked in light and dark mode. He ran it twice. Once with only the variables in the file and once with the Tokens Studio MCP that gives the agent brand context like assets and brand voice. Without brand context the pages used the variables correctly but had random text. With brand context they looked like the real brand. His advice: describe your variables. Without a description the agent picks the first variable that looks right and the design breaks when you switch modes. He also added a mode tester to the CLI that checks contrast in every mode. It is a plain function and uses no AI. “A contrast function is a no-brainer. It costs no performance, it costs no credits, we should do this locally.” One warning from his research on the Figma API: don’t stack opacity on opacity in variables. The API lets you set an opacity on a variable that references another variable even though the Figma UI doesn’t. If someone removes that opacity later the data breaks. How to install the Figma CLI Paste this URL into Claude Code and ask it to install the Figma CLI for you: https://www.intodesignsystems.com/figma-cli Then ask it what the CLI can do for your project. The Figma CLI is free and open source under the MIT license: github.com/silships/figma-cli Happy agentic designing! ✌️ Sil P.S: Want to learn how to build a CLI for your own design system? Aimee Maroney and Hannah Clarke from Deva Studios show exactly that at our AI Design Systems Conference 2027 on March 10 and 11 2027 online. Kylor Hall from Atlassian shows how Atlassian builds its AI-native design system. More speakers come from Anthropic, OpenAI, Netflix and Yahoo. The ticket includes the recording of this AI Jam. 👉 Get your ticket and watch all sessions live or with lifetime access to the recordings

wild.title: Savor of the Month (23)
wild.description: It’s November! So once again, it’s time for Savor of the Month ! For newcomers: At the start of every month I announce one specific thing or theme to look out for, pay attention to, interrogate, appreciate . The idea is to convert something everyday and taken for granted into something we might, yes, savor. And every month I create a chat thread where TAoN Supporters can share what you are noticing, or enjoy what others have noticed, in connection with the current theme. Supporters can post pictures, drawings, written observations , whatever works for you. Or just browse! Themes so far: Water (results here ) * Stripes (results here ) * Numbers (results here ) * Doors (results here ) * Pink (results here ) * Flaws (results here ) * Rust (results here ) * Public Text (results here ) * Calm (results here ) * Treasure (results here ) * Winter (results here ) * Mysteries (results here ) * Outliers (results here ) * Ornamentation (results here ) * Everyday Artists (results here ) * Reflections (results here ) * Contrast (results here ) * The Temporary (results here ; related audio essay here ) * Wind (results here ) * Circles (results here ) * Small Flowers (results here ) * Shadows (results here ) For November, the theme is BROKEN. Below, I’ll say a little more about this. But in short, whether you take pictures or write poems, or just notice your world: Be attentive to what’s BROKEN as you go about your days in the month ahead. The thread is open .
